The often overlooked discussion is that debt to GDP is not an accurate perspective. The GDP is not the same as the federal budget from tax revenue. GDP is every dollar generated by the economy. In other words, every dollar earned by private companies and individuals and government activity. That's not the same as tax revenue. In other words, if federal tax revenue is $5 million and the debt is $35 trillion, it would take over 7 years if every federal tax dolarr was used to pay down the debt. That's impossible. We still have social security and medicare payment obligations, defense, and other departments, i.e. DHS, HUD, DoE, Interior, State, HHS, DoT, Veteran Affairs, etc. We need to look at the federal debt as a 40 year mortgage. A crucial perspective is missing, though: the U.S. government, as the issuer of the dollar, can never run out of dollars to pay its bills. There's a major irony here: the very "national debt" we're told to fear is, penny for penny, the total sum of U.S. Treasuries outstanding. People like Steve Ballmer, and other ultra-wealthy individuals park a huge portion of their "liquid" wealth in these safe, interest-paying Treasuries—assets they rely on and love. Meanwhile, they often push a narrative that this same debt is a dangerous burden on everyone else. Show less Read more Like Dislike Reply @libiroli 3 months ago Great editing! How about a video on MMT next? If the US government creates dollars, why do we borrow money in the form of bonds? Why not print money, with limits on how much we create tied to a mix of inflation targets, physical resource limits & other throughput limits in the economy (factory capacity, rail throughput, barge traffic, etc)? I've been struggling with the MMT argument for a while. They approach the government as the sole source of money, discounting assets owned by wealthy individuals. And their "turn-based" model of money is nice in a world where all dollars are paid by the government into the economy then all end back with the government, with no clear picture of what happens with money circulating in the economy that may linger for years or decades in private hands. And there's no clear model for limits on MMT before inflation happens - sems like you gotta keep spending until you hit the limit. Maybe there's a mathematical model just waiting to solve this, but I'm unaware of it currently. The secret bridge between MMT & today's bond-based financing? Bonds held by the Fed are essentially 0% interest, because the Fed remits any profits on operations to the US Treasury. It's one powerful tool in a solution, but much more must be developed. My fear is MMT may fail horribly, because the limits may not be fully knowable nor enforceable on Congress. In this episode of Just the Facts, Steve Ballmer breaks down the data behind America’s national debt using official U.S. government sources. The U.S. national debt now exceeds $38 trillion, the highest level in history. But that number alone doesn’t explain what the debt is, how it grew, or what it means for the economy. This video explains how annual budget deficits add up over time, why the federal government borrows money, and how interest payments have become one of the largest federal expenses. You’ll also learn the difference between debt held by the public and intragovernmental debt, who owns U.S. debt today, and how much of it is held by Americans versus foreign investors.
